newsitem.title: FRANCE: French truckers keen on talks, protest continues.
newsitem.headline: French truckers keen on talks, protest continues.

text.p: French truck drivers' union leaders said on Friday they were keen to negotiate an end to a 12-day-old strike that is strangling the economy provided the government guaranteed by decree payment for all hours worked.
Prime Minister Alain Juppe called for an urgent solution, cautioning that "the consequences (of a prolonged strike) on our economy, on many companies, on many workers risk being very damaging".
He ruled out using force to clear truckers' blockades at 230 main roads and almost half the country's petrol depots.
As junior transport minister Anne-Marie Idrac promised a decree within two weeks to define working hours, unions and haulage bosses met at the Transport Ministry to sign a deal on early retirement.
"We don't want to prolong the strike artificially," said Claude Debons of the biggest union, the Socialist-led CFDT. "The condition for lifting the roadblocks is a guarantee on working hours."

"We have come to seek a clear reply from the government on working time. If we have to work all day, we'll work all day," said Alain Renault, representative of the second largest union among the truckers, the Communist-led CGT.

Unions and employers were due to sign agreements on early retirement at 55 instead of 60 for drivers with 25 years at the wheel, sick pay, travel expenses and a ban on Sunday driving reached during a talks this week.

But the related issues of pay and hours remained outstanding when those talks broke down on Thursday. Full payment for all hours worked, including unloading time and compulsory rest periods on the road, would be equivalent to a substantial pay rise.

"People have said for years that the issue (of working hours) must be settled and we need to go further. We must clarify in an irrefutable manner what working hours should involve, what should be paid for. We need a decree," Idrac said.
Truckers say they often work more than 200 hours a month, with many hours unpaid as they wait to load and unload.

But Idrac insisted pay was an issue for unions and bosses and not for the government. Unions demand pay hikes of an average 23 percent. Employers have offered a one percent real pay rise and a 1,500 franc ($300) one-time bonus.

Bosses said that while they could not increase their offer, they would be flexible in re-arranging its terms. Employers' spokesman Rene Petit said raising the pay offer would ruin many haulage companies.

In southern Corsica, truckers and haulage bosses conducting separate negotiations agreed overnight on a monthly wage hike of 580 francs ($116). Truckers lifted a blockade of Ajaccio's main petrol depot on Friday.
The strike, in the crucial pre-Christmas commercial period, has cost European food and haulage industries tens of millions of dollars a day, prompting protests from France's neighbours.
Truckers have also sealed off the country's 13 oil refineries. Petrol rationing has spread and about 5,000 of 18,000 petrol stations were either dry or feeling shortages.
The roadblocks have forced the closures of some factories for lack of supplies and cut deliveries of perishable goods ranging from fish to fruit and flowers.
The blockade stranded up to 14,000 Spanish trucks and idled about 90 percent of Portugal's total truck fleet. Belgian ports were clogged by British-bound lorries avoiding France.
